plain_english: A free person lives how they want to live. They're not forced, blocked, or pushed around. Their actions flow naturally. They get what they want and avoid what they don't want. So who chooses to live in error? Nobody. Who chooses to live deceived, prone to mistakes, unfair, out of control, unhappy, or petty? Nobody. None of the bad people live as they wish. So they're not free. Who chooses to live in grief, fear, envy, or pity? Who chooses to want things and not get them, or to try avoiding something and fall right into it? Nobody. Do we find any bad people who are free from grief and fear? Any who avoid what they don't want and get what they do want? Not one. So we don't find any bad people who are free.
original_excerpt: He is free who lives as he wishes to live; who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance, nor to force; whose movements to action ([Greek: hormai]) are not impeded, whose desires attain their purpose, and who does not fall into that which he would avoid ([Greek: echchliseis aperiptotoi]). Who then chooses to live in error? No man. Who chooses to live deceived, liable to mistake, unjust, unrestrained, discontented, mean? No man. Not one then of the bad lives as he wishes; nor is he then free. And who chooses to live in sorrow, fear, envy, pity, desiring and failing in his desires, attempting to avoid something and falling into it? Not one. Do we then find any of the bad free from sorrow, free from fear, who does not fall into that which he would avoid, and does not obtain that which he wishes? Not one; nor then do we find any bad man free.

plain_english: Now answer this: Does freedom seem great and noble and valuable to you? Of course it does. So when someone gets something this great and valuable and noble, can they act like a coward? No way. When you see someone bowing to another person or flattering them against their own beliefs, say confidently that this person is not free. It doesn't matter if they're doing it for a free meal or for a government position or high office. Call the people who do this for small things "little slaves." Call the ones who do it for big things "great slaves" — because that's what they are. You agree with this, right? Do you think freedom means being independent and self-governing? Absolutely. So anyone who can be stopped or forced by another person — declare that they are not free.
original_excerpt: Further, then, answer me this question, also: does freedom seem to you to be something great and noble and valuable? How should it not seem so? Is it possible then when a man obtains anything so great and valuable and noble to be mean? It is not possible. When then you see any man subject to another or flattering him contrary to his own opinion, confidently affirm that this man also is not free; and not only if he do this for a bit of supper, but also if he does it for a government (province) or a consulship; and call these men little slaves who for the sake of little matters do these things, and those who do so for the sake of great things call great slaves, as they deserve to be. This is admitted also. Do you think that freedom is a thing independent and self-governing? Certainly. Whomsoever then it is in the power of another to hinder and compel, declare that he is not free.

plain_english: Don't worry about someone's family background or whether they were born free or enslaved. Listen to what they actually say. If you hear them calling anyone "Master" from the heart — even if they're a consul with all the official honors — call them a slave. If you hear them saying "Poor me, look how much I suffer," call them a slave. If you see them complaining, whining, or miserable, call them a slave, even if they wear the finest clothes. But if they don't do any of these things, don't assume they're free yet. Check their beliefs. Are their thoughts controlled by outside forces? Can external things mess with their peace of mind? Can bad luck ruin them? If so, call them a slave on vacation — like during Saturnalia when slaves get a brief break. Their master is just away for now. He'll be back soon, and then you'll see what they really endure.
original_excerpt: And do not look, I entreat you, after his grandfathers and great-grandfathers, or inquire about his being bought or sold, but if you hear him saying from his heart and with feeling, "Master," even if the twelve fasces precede him (as consul), call him a slave. And if you hear him say, "Wretch that I am, how much I suffer," call him a slave. If, finally, you see him lamenting, complaining, unhappy, call him a slave, though he wears a praetexta. If, then, he is doing nothing of this kind do not yet say that he is free, but learn his opinions, whether they are subject to compulsion, or may produce hindrance, or to bad fortune, and if you find him such, call him a slave who has a holiday in the Saturnalia; say that his master is from home; he will return soon, and you will know what he suffers.

plain_english: So what makes a person truly free and in charge of their own life? Money doesn't do it. Neither does being a consul, ruling a province, or having royal power. There must be something else. What makes you free and unblocked when you're writing? Knowing how to write. What about when you're playing the lute? Knowing how to play the lute. So in life, it must be knowing how to live. You've heard this in general terms. But let's look at the details. Can someone who wants things that depend on other people be free from obstacles? No. Can they be unblocked? No. So they can't be free. Think about this: do we have nothing that's completely under our control? Or do we control everything? Or do we control some things while others control other things?
original_excerpt: What then is that which makes a man free from hindrance and makes him his own master? For wealth does not do it, nor consulship, nor provincial government, nor royal power; but something else must be discovered. What then is that which when we write makes us free from hindrance and unimpeded? The knowledge of the art of writing. What then is it in playing the lute? The science of playing the lute. Therefore in life also it is the science of life. You have then heard in a general way; but examine the thing also in the several parts. Is it possible that he who desires any of the things which depend on others can be free from hindrance? No. Is it possible for him to be unimpeded? No. Therefore he cannot be free. Consider then, whether we have nothing which is in our own power only, or whether we have all things, or whether some things are in our own power, and others in the power of others.

plain_english: What do you mean? When you want your body to be whole and sound, is that up to you or not? It's not up to me. When you want it to be healthy? That's not up to me either. When you want it to be attractive? Not that either. Life or death? That's not up to me. So your body belongs to someone else — it's subject to anyone stronger than you. It is. But your property — is it up to you to have it when you want, for as long as you want, exactly as you want? No. And your slaves? No. And your clothes? No. And your house? No. And your horses? Not one of these things. And if you desperately want your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends — is that up to you? This also is not up to me.
original_excerpt: What do you mean? When you wish the body to be entire (sound) is it in your power or not? It is not in my power. When you wish it to be healthy? Neither is this in my power. When you wish it to be handsome? Nor is this. Life or death? Neither is this in my power. Your body then is another's, subject to every man who is stronger than yourself. It is. But your estate is it in your power to have it when you please, and as long as you please, and such as you please? No. And your slaves? No. And your clothes? No. And your house? No. And your horses? Not one of these things. And if you wish by all means your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends, is it in your power? This also is not in my power.

plain_english: Do you have anything that belongs completely to you? Something that depends only on you and can't be taken away? I don't know. Let's look at this and figure it out. Can anyone force you to believe something false? No one can. So when it comes to what you believe, you're free. No one can stop you. Agreed? Good. Now, can someone force you to want something you don't actually want? Yes, he can. When he threatens me with death or prison, he makes me want to move toward what he wants. But what if you don't fear death or prison? Do you still care what he thinks? No. So is not fearing death your own action, or isn't it? It's my own action.
original_excerpt: Whether then have you nothing which is in your own power, which depends on yourself only and cannot be taken from you, or have you anything of the kind? I know not. Look at the thing then thus, and examine it. Is any man able to make you assent to that which is false? No man. In the matter of assent then you are free from hindrance and obstruction. Granted. Well; and can a man force you to desire to move towards that to which you do not choose? He can, for when he threatens me with death or bonds he compels me to desire to move towards it. If then you despise death and bonds, do you still pay any regard to him? No. Is then the despising of death an act of your own or is it not yours? It is my act.

plain_english: Once you've prepared yourself and practiced this discipline — separating what belongs to others from what's yours, what can be blocked from what can't be blocked, focusing only on what can't be blocked and ignoring what can be — do you still fear anyone? No. What would you be afraid of? The things that are truly yours, where good and evil actually exist? Who has power over those? Who can take them away or stop them? No one can — any more than they can stop God. But are you going to be afraid about your body and your stuff? Things that aren't really yours? Things that don't actually concern you?
original_excerpt: When you have made this preparation, and have practised this discipline, to distinguish that which belongs to another from that which is your own, the things which are subject to hindrance from those which are not, to consider the things free from hindrance to concern yourself, and those which are not free not to concern yourself, to keep your desire steadily fixed to the things which do concern yourself, and turned from the things which do not concern yourself; do you still fear any man? No one. For about what will you be afraid? About the things which are your own, in which consists the nature of good and evil? and who has power over these things? who can take them away? who can impede them? No man can, no more than he can impede God. But will you be afraid about your body and your possessions, about things which are not yours, about things which in no way concern you?

plain_english: What else have you been studying all along? You've been learning to tell the difference between what's yours and what's not yours. What's in your power and what's not. What can be blocked and what can't. So why did you come to the philosophers? Was it so you could still be miserable and unhappy? If you do what I'm assuming you've done, you'll be without fear and worry. And what is grief to you then? Fear comes from what you expect to happen. Grief comes from what's happening now. But what more could you want? For the things that are within your control — the good things that are here now — you have proper, well-ordered desires. For the things outside your control, you don't want any of them. So you don't give any room to what's irrational, impatient, and way too hasty.
original_excerpt: and what else have you been studying from the beginning than to distinguish between your own and not your own, the things which are in your power and not in your power, the things subject to hindrance and not subject? and why have you come to the philosophers? was it that you may nevertheless be unfortunate and unhappy? You will then in this way, as I have supposed you to have done, be without fear and disturbance. And what is grief to you? for fear comes from what you expect, but grief from that which is present. But what further will you desire? For of the things which are within the power of the will, as being good and present, you have a proper and regulated desire; but of the things which are not in the power of the will you do not desire any one, and so you do not allow any place to that which is irrational, and impatient, and above measure hasty.

plain_english: You've received everything from someone else — even your own self. So why do you get angry and blame the giver when he takes something back from you? Who are you? What are you here for? Didn't God bring you into this world? Didn't he show you the light? Didn't he give you people to work alongside, and senses, and the ability to think? And what did he make you? He made you mortal. He put you on earth with a little bit of flesh. You're here to watch how he runs things and to join in his show and celebration for a short time. When your time is up and he calls you to leave, won't you go with respect and gratitude for everything you've seen and heard? No — you say you want to keep enjoying the party. People at religious ceremonies would also like to stay longer. People at the Olympic games would like to see more athletes compete. But the ceremony is over. Leave like a grateful and humble person. Make room for others. Other people need to be born, just like you were. And once they're born, they need space and homes and the things they require. If the first people never leave, what's left for the rest? Why can't you ever have enough? Why aren't you satisfied? Why are you trying to squeeze the world tight? 'But I want my children and my wife with me.'
original_excerpt: Then after receiving everything from another and even yourself, are you angry and do you blame the giver if he takes anything from you? Who are you, and for what purpose did you come into the world? Did not he (God) introduce you here, did he not show you the light, did he not give you fellow-workers, and perceptions and reason? and as whom did he introduce you here? did he not introduce you as subject to death, and as one to live on the earth with a little flesh, and to observe his administration, and to join with him in the spectacle and the festival for a short time? Will you not then, as long as you have been permitted, after seeing the spectacle and the solemnity, when he leads you out, go with adoration of him and thanks for what you have heard and seen? No; but I would still enjoy the feast. The initiated too would wish to be longer in the initiation; and perhaps also those at Olympia to see other athletes. But the solemnity is ended; go away like a grateful and modest man; make room for others; others also must be born, as you were, and, being born, they must have a place, and houses, and necessary things. And if the first do not retire, what remains? Why are you insatiable? Why are you not content? why do you contract the world? Yes, but I would have my little children with me and my wife.

plain_english: What, are these things yours? Don't they belong to whoever gave them to you and made you? Then why won't you give up what belongs to others? Why won't you step aside for someone who's superior? "But why did he bring me into the world under these conditions?" If you don't like the conditions, leave. He doesn't need a spectator who complains. He wants people who join the celebration, who take part in the chorus, who applaud and admire and sing praises for the occasion. But those who can't handle any trouble, the cowards — he won't mind if they skip the great gathering. When they were there, they didn't act like they should at a festival. They didn't fill their role properly. Instead they whined, complained about God, about fortune, about their companions. They couldn't see what they had or their own powers, which they received for the opposite purpose — powers of courage, generosity, strong spirit, and what we're talking about now: freedom. So why did I receive these things? To use them. For how long? As long as whoever lent them decides. "But what if I need them?" Don't attach yourself to them and you won't need them. Don't tell yourself they're necessary, and then they won't be necessary.
original_excerpt: What, are they yours? do they not belong to the giver, and to him who made you? then will you not give up what belongs to others? will you not give way to him who is superior? Why then did he introduce me into the world on these conditions? And if the conditions do not suit you, depart. He has no need of a spectator who is not satisfied. He wants those who join in the festival, those who take part in the chorus, that they may rather applaud, admire, and celebrate with hymns the solemnity. But those who can bear no trouble, and the cowardly, he will not unwillingly see absent from the great assembly ([Greek: panaeguris]) for they did not when they were present behave as they ought to do at a festival nor fill up their place properly, but they lamented, found fault with the deity, fortune, their companions; not seeing both what they had, and their own powers, which they received for contrary purposes, the powers of magnanimity, of a generous mind, manly spirit, and what we are now inquiring about, freedom. For what purpose then have I received these things? To use them. How long? So long as he who has lent them chooses. What if they are necessary to me? Do not attach yourself to them and they will not be necessary; do not say to yourself that they are necessary, and then they are not necessary.

plain_english: You might ask me, "Are you free then?" I wish I were, and I pray to be free. But I'm not there yet. I can't face my masters. I still value this poor body of mine. I care deeply about keeping it intact, even though I don't truly own it. But I can show you someone who was free, so you don't have to keep looking for an example. Diogenes was free. How was he free? Not because his parents were free, but because he made himself free. He threw off everything that could enslave him. No one could get close enough to grab him and make him a slave. Everything he had was loose in his grip, barely attached to him. If you grabbed his possessions, he would have let them go rather than chase after you. If you grabbed his leg, he would have let go of his leg. If you took his whole body, his whole poor body — fine. Same with his close friends, his buddies, his country. He knew where all these things came from, who gave them to him, and under what conditions.
original_excerpt: You then, a man may say, are you free? I wish, by the gods, and pray to be free; but I am not yet able to face my masters, I still value my poor body, I value greatly the preservation of it entire, though I do not possess it entire. But I can point out to you a free man, that you may no longer seek an example. Diogenes was free. How was he free? Not because he was born of free parents, but because he was himself free, because he had cast off all the handles of slavery, and it was not possible for any man to approach him, nor had any man the means of laying hold of him to enslave him. He had everything easily loosed, everything only hanging to him. If you laid hold of his property, he would have rather let it go and be yours, than he would have followed you for it; if you had laid hold of his leg, he would have let go his leg; if of all his body, all his poor body; his intimates, friends, country, just the same. For he knew from whence he had them, and from whom, and on what conditions.

plain_english: His true parents were the gods, and his real country was the universe. He would never abandon them. He obeyed them more than anyone else. No one would die for his country more willingly. He didn't question when he was serving the whole universe. He remembered that everything comes from there and serves that country, commanded by whoever runs it. So look at what Diogenes himself says: "This is why, Diogenes, you can speak to the King of Persia and to King Archidamus of Sparta however you want." Was this because he had free parents? I guess all Athenians and Spartans, born from slaves, couldn't talk to these kings as they wished. They were afraid and sucked up to them instead. So why does he say he has this power? "Because I don't think this poor body belongs to me. Because I want nothing. Because law is everything to me, and nothing else matters." These things made him free.
original_excerpt: His true parents indeed, the gods, and his real country he would never have deserted, nor would he have yielded to any man in obedience to them and to their orders, nor would any man have died for his country more readily. For he was not used to inquire when he should be considered to have done anything on behalf of the whole of things (the universe, or all the world), but he remembered that everything which is done comes from thence and is done on behalf of that country and is commanded by him who administers it. Therefore see what Diogenes himself says and writes: "For this reason," he says, "Diogenes, it is in your power to speak both with the King of the Persians and with Archidamus the King of the Lacedaemonians, as you please." Was it because he was born of free parents? I suppose all the Athenians and all the Lacedaemonians, because they were born of slaves, could not talk with them (these kings) as they wished, but feared and paid court to them. Why then does he say that it is in his power? Because I do not consider the poor body to be my own, because I want nothing, because law is everything to me, and nothing else is. These were the things which permitted him to be free.

plain_english: Think about these ideas, these beliefs, these words. Look at these examples if you want to be free — if you really want freedom for what it's worth. Why be surprised that something so valuable costs so much? People have hanged themselves for what they call liberty. Others have thrown themselves off cliffs. Sometimes entire cities have died for it. So why won't you give back to God what he gave you when he asks for it — all for true, unshakeable, secure freedom? Why won't you do what Plato says: learn not just to die, but to endure torture, exile, beatings — in short, to give up everything that isn't really yours? If you won't do this, you'll be a slave among slaves. Even if you become consul ten thousand times. Even if you make it to Caesar's palace. You'll still be a slave. And you'll realize that maybe philosophers say things that go against popular opinion — paradoxes, as Cleanthes called them — but not things that go against reason.
original_excerpt: Think of these things, these opinions, these words; look to these examples, if you would be free, if you desire the thing according to its worth. And what is the wonder if you buy so great a thing at the price of things so many and so great? For the sake of this which is called liberty, some hang themselves, others throw themselves down precipices, and sometimes even whole cities have perished; and will you not for the sake of the true and unassailable and secure liberty give back to God when he demands them the things which he has given? Will you not, as Plato says, study not to die only, but also to endure torture, and exile, and scourging, and, in a word, to give up all which is not your own? If you will not, you will be a slave among slaves, even if you be ten thousand times a consul; and if you make your way up to the palace (Cæsar's residence), you will no less be a slave; and you will feel that perhaps philosophers utter words which are contrary to common opinion (paradoxes), as Cleanthes also said, but not words contrary to reason.

plain_english:
You'll learn from experience that these words are true. The things people value and chase after don't actually benefit those who get them. And for those who don't have them yet, there's this fantasy that once they get these things, everything good will come with them. But when they finally get them, the restless feeling is still there. The tossing and turning is still there. The dissatisfaction is still there. The wanting what you don't have is still there. You don't get freedom by fully possessing the things you want. You get it by removing the wanting itself. 

To prove this is true, put the same effort into philosophy that you put into chasing those other things. Stay alert to develop beliefs that will make you free. Court a philosopher instead of some rich old man. Be seen hanging around a philosopher's door. You won't embarrass yourself by being seen there. You won't leave empty-handed or without gain — if you approach the philosopher the right way. And if you don't succeed, at least try. The attempt itself is not shameful.
original_excerpt: For you will know by experience that the words are true, and that there is no profit from the things which are valued and eagerly sought to those who have obtained them; and to those who have not yet obtained them there is an imagination ([Greek: phantasia]), that when these things are come, all that is good will come with them; then, when they are come, the feverish feeling is the same, the tossing to and fro is the same, the satiety, the desire of things, which are not present; for freedom is acquired not by the full possession of the things which are desired, but by removing the desire. And that you may know that this is true, as you have labored for those things, so transfer your labor to these: be vigilant for the purpose of acquiring an opinion which will make you free; pay court to a philosopher instead of to a rich old man; be seen about a philosopher's doors; you will not disgrace yourself by being seen; you will not go away empty nor without profit, if you go to the philosopher as you ought, and if not (if you do not succeed), try at least; the trial (attempt) is not disgraceful.
